objective: Design and implement infrastructure as code (IaC)
stem: Two teams deploy Bicep to the same resource group. One deployment removed a resource the other team owns. Which deployment mode caused this?

options.text: Complete mode, which deletes resources in the group that are not in the template
Incremental mode, which reconciles the group against the template
Validate mode, which rolls back unrecognised resources
What-if mode, which applies the previewed deletions

explanation: Complete mode treats the template as the full definition of the resource group and deletes anything not declared in it. Incremental — the default — leaves unlisted resources alone, which is why shared resource groups should stay on incremental.

whyWrong.B: Incremental never deletes resources missing from the template.
whyWrong.D: What-if only previews; it applies nothing.

hint: One of these modes reconciles the group against the template in both directions. Ask which, and what that does to resources the template never mentions.

objective: Design and implement infrastructure as code (IaC)
stem: Where should Terraform state live when the plan and apply run from an Azure Pipelines agent?

options.text: A remote backend such as an Azure Storage blob container, with state locking enabled
On the agent's working directory, published as a pipeline artifact
Committed to the repository alongside the `.tf` files
In a pipeline variable group as a secret

explanation: Agents are ephemeral and several runs may overlap, so state has to be shared and locked externally. Azure Storage backends use blob leases for locking, which prevents two applies corrupting the same state.

whyWrong.B: Agent-local state disappears with the agent and does not lock across concurrent runs.
whyWrong.C: State contains secrets in plain text and would conflict on every merge.
whyWrong.D: Variable groups hold small values and cannot be written back to during a run.

docs.title: Store Terraform state in Azure Storage

stem: A pipeline builds a container image and must tag it so any running container can be traced back to the exact build. Which tag serves that best?

options.text: The build id or the commit SHA, alongside a moving `latest` tag
`latest` only, since it always points at the newest build
The branch name, so the environment is obvious
The date the image was built

explanation: An immutable, unique tag is what makes an image traceable — you can map a running container straight back to a build and a commit. `latest` is convenient for humans but ambiguous, since it means something different tomorrow.

whyWrong.B: `latest` cannot identify which build is actually running.
whyWrong.C: A branch produces many builds, so the tag is not unique.
whyWrong.D: Multiple builds happen on the same day, so the date is not unique either.

docs.title: Recommendations for tagging and versioning images

stem: A pipeline deploys to AKS. If the new pods never pass their readiness probes, the previous version must keep serving traffic. Which approach gives that natively?

options.text: A Kubernetes rolling update, which halts and leaves the previous ReplicaSet serving traffic if new pods never become ready
Deleting the Deployment and recreating it from the new manifest
Scaling the Deployment to zero before applying the new image
Applying the manifest with `kubectl replace --force`

explanation: A rolling update only replaces old pods as new ones report ready, so a failing readiness probe stalls the rollout with the previous version still serving. `kubectl rollout undo` then returns to the last good revision.

whyWrong.B: Deleting first means there is nothing left to serve traffic during the failure.
whyWrong.C: Scaling to zero causes an outage and discards the fallback.
whyWrong.D: `--force` deletes and recreates the resource, losing the safety of the gradual rollout.

hint: Kubernetes will not take an old pod out of service until a new one reports ready. Which strategy relies on that, and which ones remove the old version first?

stem: A nightly pipeline fails only when it runs on one particular self-hosted agent. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: That agent's software or environment has drifted from the others
The pipeline YAML contains a syntax error
The schedule is set to the wrong time zone
The repository has diverged from main

explanation: A failure that follows one agent points at that agent, not the pipeline. Hand-maintained agents drift; the durable fix is to build agents from an image or run them as containers so every agent is identical.

whyWrong.B: A YAML error would fail on every agent.
whyWrong.C: A wrong time zone changes when it runs, not whether it passes.
whyWrong.D: Repository state is the same regardless of which agent picks up the job.

stem: Pipeline runs queue for long periods while agents sit idle in another pool. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the pipeline's demands match the capabilities of agents in the pool it targets
Whether the organisation has enough parallel jobs purchased
Whether the repository is too large to clone
Whether the build has too many stages

explanation: A job waits when no agent in its pool satisfies its demands. Idle agents elsewhere are irrelevant — pools are the unit of allocation, and demands are matched against agent capabilities within the targeted pool.

whyWrong.B: Parallelism limits are worth checking, but they would not leave agents idle in the pool being targeted.
whyWrong.C: Clone size affects run duration, not queue time.
whyWrong.D: Stage count affects how many jobs are queued, not whether an agent can accept them.

objective: Design and implement a package management strategy
stem: A package should be visible to a pilot team for testing, and only promoted to everyone once it is signed off. Which Azure Artifacts feature does this?

options.text: Feed views, promoting a package version from `@Prerelease` to `@Release`
Upstream sources, adding the feed as an upstream of itself
Retention policies, keeping only reviewed versions
A separate organisation for the pilot team

explanation: Views are filtered slices of a feed. Consumers subscribe to a view, and promoting a version into `@Release` publishes it to that audience without republishing the package — the artifact stays byte-identical.

whyWrong.B: Upstreams pull packages in from elsewhere and have nothing to do with promotion.
whyWrong.C: Retention deletes old versions; it does not control visibility.
whyWrong.D: A second organisation duplicates everything and breaks traceability.

hint: The package itself does not change when it is signed off — only who can see it. Which feature filters what a consumer of the feed is shown?

objective: Design and implement a testing strategy for pipelines
stem: Which two practices most improve the speed of the feedback loop for developers? Choose two.

options.text: Run fast unit tests and static analysis on the pull request build
Parallelise the test suite across multiple agents
Move all tests to a nightly run so PR builds stay short
Increase the pull request reviewer requirement to three people
Publish test results only when the build fails

explanation: Shift-left plus parallelisation is the standard answer: catch what you can cheaply on the PR, and cut wall-clock time by splitting the suite. Both shorten the gap between writing a defect and learning about it.

whyWrong.C: This makes PR builds fast but delays every failure by up to a day.
whyWrong.E: Withholding results on success removes trend data such as coverage and duration.

hint: Feedback speed has two levers: catching things earlier, and taking less wall-clock time to catch them. Two options pull those levers; the rest push work later.
